pride_data.title: Deciphering the architecture and interactome of the spliceosomal C complex using in vivo chemical crosslinking
pride_data.projectDescription: We used in vivo PIR-based crosslinking to assess specific regions of interaction and protein structure of the spliceosomal C complex components hnRNPA1, A2/B1, and C, and the RALY protein. Our results indicate the interaction of proteins of the C complex via domains regions and conserved motifs, posing as evidence of a coordinated action of known regulatory sequences of RBPs. Moreover, the crosslinking information helped to model some of the RBPs, being complementary to other structural methods available.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Cell lysis HeLa cells were seeded at a density of 5 × 106 cells into 150 mm culture dishes with 20 ml of DMEM supplemented with 10% dialyzed fetal bovine serum (Valley Biomedical) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin (Fisher Scientific). Cells were harvested with 5 ml of PBS 1× with 5 mM EDTA for 3 min, at 37 °C. Cells were washed once with a solution containing 1 mM CaCl2 and 1 mM MgCl2 and twice with PBS 1×, pelleted each time by centrifugation at 300 × g for 3 min. Cell pellets were suspended in 1 mL of HEPES buffer (200 mM HEPES, 200 mM NaCl, 2 mM EDTA, pH 7.5) and cryo-milled using the Mixer Mill MM 400 (Retsch), following the manufacturer’s instructions. The cell powder was suspended in 500 μL of HEPES buffer. Chemical crosslinking Two biological replicates of each cell lysate – treated with RNase and control – were crosslinked with the PIR crosslinker amide BDP-NHP, as previously described 12,13. Briefly, 10 mM of amide BDP-NHP in 500 μL of crosslinker buffer (170 mM Na2HPO4, pH 8.0) was added to the cell lysates and the reaction happened for 30 min, in room temperature with constant shaking. The crosslinked cells were pelleted by centrifugation at 300 × g for 3 min and washed 3 times with PBS 1×. Sample preparation Crosslinked cell pellets were suspended in 8 M urea solution in 0.1M NH4HCO3 buffer, pH 8.0, and sonicated using a GE-130 ultrasonic processor, followed by reduction, alkylation, and tryptic digestion. Peptide samples were acidified to pH 2 with trifluoroacetic acid, followed by desalting by solid phase extraction using C18 Sep-Pak cartridges (Waters) and concentration by vacuum centrifugation. Resulting peptides were suspended in 500 μL of solvent A (7 mM KH2PO4, 30% acetonitrile pH 2.8) and fractionated by SCX chromatography using an Agilent 1200 series high-performance liquid chromatography system equipped with a 250 3 10.0 mm column packed with Luna 5 mm diameter, 100 A ° pore size particles (Phenomenex). Peptide separation was made using a binary mobile phase solvent system consisting of solvent A and solvent B (7 mM KH2PO4, 350 mM KCl, 30% acetonitrile pH 2.8) at a flow rate of 1.5 mL/min using the following gradient program: 0-7.5 min 100% A, 7.5-47.5 min 95% A/5% B to 40% A/ 60% B, 47.5- 67.5 min 40% A/ 60% B to 100% B, 67.5-77.5 min 100% B, 77.5-97.5 min 100% A. A total of 14 fractions were collected and pooled as follows: fractions 1 to 5, 6 and 7, and 11 to 14. Crosslinked peptides from SCX fractions were further enriched using UltraLink monomeric avidin (Thermo). The enriched crosslinked peptide sample was concentrated by vacuum centrifugation and stored at 80 °C. LC-MS/MS analysis of cross-linked samples Pooled peptides from SCX fractions (1-5, 6-7, 8, 9, 10, and 11-14) were suspended in 30 μL of 0.1% (vol/vol) formic acid. Sample fractions were centrifuged at 16,000 × g for 10 min at room temperature and the supernatant of each sample transferred to an LC autosampler vials (Thermo). For the LC-MS/MS analysis, 3 µL of each sample (approximately 1 µg) from each pooled fraction was injected into the nano-LC system (Thermo), coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo). Each fraction was analyzed 2 times for technical replicates of the experiment. Each peptide fraction was then loaded onto a trap column [3 cm × 100-μm i.d., stationary phase ReproSil-Pur C8 (5-μm diameter and 120-Å-pore-size particles)] with a flow rate of 2 μL/min of mobile phase: 98% (vol/vol) LC–MS solvent A [0.1% (vol/vol) FA in water] and 2% (vol/vol) LC–MS solvent B [0.1% (vol/vol) FA in acetonitrile], and chromatographically separated using an analytical column [60 cm × 75-μm i.d., stationary phase ReproSil-Pur C8 (5-μm diameter and 120-Å-pore-size particles)], applying a 240-min linear gradient: from 95% LC–MS solvent A, 5% LC–MS solvent B to 60% LC–MS solvent A, 40% LC–MS solvent B, at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. For Mango analysis of the PIR crosslinker 14, the mass spectrometer was set to high resolution method to data-dependent acquisition (DDA) of the 5 most intense ions with charge state of +4 to +8, with a dynamic exclusion of 30 s and isolation window of 3 Da. Each MS1 scan (70,000 resolving power at 200 m/z, automated gain control (AGC) of 1 × 106, scan range 400 to 2,000 m/z, dynamic exclusion of 30 s) was followed by 5 MS2 scans (70,000 resolving power at 200 m/z, AGC of 5 × 104, normalized collision energy of 30).

passages.text: Deciphering the architecture and interactome of hnRNP proteins

RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) have conserved domains and consensus sequences that interact with RNAs and other proteins forming ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes. RNPs are involved in the regulation of several cellular processes, including transcription, pre-mRNA splicing, mRNA transport, localization, degradation and storage, and ultimately control of translation. Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) comprise a family of RBPs that mediate transcription control and nuclear processing of transcripts. Some hnRNPs are part of the spliceosome complex, a dynamic machinery formed by RNPs that regulate alternative splicing of pre-mRNAs. Here, chemical crosslinking of proteins was applied to identify specific interacting regions and protein structural features of hnRNPs: hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, hnRNPC, and RALY. The results reveal interaction of these proteins within RNA-binding domains and conserved motifs, providing evidence of a coordinated action of known regulatory sequences of RBPs. Moreover, these crosslinking data enable structural model generation for RBPs, illustrating how cross-linking mass spectrometry can complement other structural methods.
Graphical Abstract
INTRODUCTION

RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are involved in the regulation of many cellular processes, including pre-mRNA splicing, RNA editing in the nucleus, translation regulation in the cytoplasm, and ultimately the control of RNA storage and degradation in stress granules and P-bodies. RBPs bind to specific regions of RNAs and interact with other regulatory proteins via conserved RNA-binding domains (RBDs), e.g., the RNA-recognition motif (RRM), one of the most abundant domains in eukaryotic cells, and regulate the processing in the nucleus, stability, localization, and translation of target transcripts in the cytoplasm. The RRM domain has approximately 90 amino acids and participates in RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions. This domain comprises two highly conserved motifs related to RNA-binding specificity, the RNP1, located in the β3 strand, and the RNP2, in the β1 strand. The consensus sequences of RNP1 and RNP2 are (R/K)-G-(F/Y)-(G/A)-(F/Y)-V-X-(F/Y) and (L/I)-(F/Y)-(V/I)-X-(N/G)-L, respectively.

Complexes formed by RNAs and regulatory proteins are known as ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes, which ultimately determine the fate of its target transcripts in the cell. RNPs include the heterogeneous nuclear RNPs (hnRNPs) protein family, comprised by approximately 20 RBPs, from hnRNP A1 to U, with different RNA-binding domains and functions; these isoforms result from alternative transcript splicing and post-translational modifications. hnRNPs regulate key cellular mechanisms, such as DNA repair, cell signaling, apoptosis, angiogenesis, telomere function control, and cell invasion, with evidence of an important role in many cancer types. hnRNPs are part of the spliceosome, a dynamic machinery responsible for controlling a highly regulated process in the nucleus of eukaryotic cells, the alternative splicing of transcripts. Despite having key roles in RNA metabolism and regulation in the nucleus, much is yet to be discovered on how hnRNPs interact in RNP complexes to ultimately regulate the fate of RNAs.

Because a large number of RBPs, including hnRNPs, present disordered regions in their sequence, available protein structures usually comprise ordered domains, e.g., RRMs. To overcome this limitation, recent studies have used chemical crosslinking of proteins to assess the structure and interactions of RBPs. These include studies on ribosomal proteins, e.g., the 70S ribosomal unit, the ribosome post-recycling complex, and the bacterial protein S1. More recently, in-solution chemical crosslinking was used to analyze the structure of the splicing factor Spp2 and its interaction with the DEAH-box ATPase Prp2. However, the vast majority of studies about RBPs using crosslinking focus on RNA-protein interactions using well stablished methods, e.g., UV crosslinking, that could be coupled to immunoprecipitation (CLIP). For protein complexes studies, a common approach is to isolate RBP complexes using immunoprecipitation assays or fractionation strategies for complex isolation followed by LC-MS analysis. While these methods are informative on complex composition, the initial isolation step limits information to protein-protein interactions that survive co-purification.

To investigate structures and interactions of hnRNPs, crosslinking and mass spectrometry studies with HeLa cell lysates were performed using a protein interaction reporter (PIR)-based crosslinker, the amide BDP-NHP (Figure 1). This approach allowed for the identification of interlinks between the hnRNP proteins hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, hnRNPC, and RALY, components of the spliceosomal C complex, shedding light on interactions of hnRNPs. The crosslinks identified in these studies, in combination with data from other structural methodologies – e.g., X-ray crystallography, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM)– were key to structural models of regulatory regions of these RBPs that were then further useful for larger complex assemblies. Moreover, most of the links identified in the proteins hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, hnRNPC, and RALY were observed in regions of the RRM domain and other conserved motifs and consensus sequences, suggesting a coordinated mechanism of action of known regulatory sequences of RBPs.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this study, chemical crosslinking and mass spectrometry (XL-MS) technologies were applied to HeLa cell lysates (in vitro) using the PIR-based crosslinker amide BDP-NHP. The in silico analysis of the crosslinking data allowed for the identification of 2,207 non-redundant crosslinks, with estimated 1% FDR and probability>0.5, corresponding to 795 protein pairs and 17% of inter-protein links (interlinks). The dataset comprises a total of 1,364 crosslinks specific for RNA-binding proteins, with 18% of interlinks, corresponding to 1,206 site pairs and 398 protein pairs. The complete crosslinking information is made available in Supplementary material 1 and in the interaction table available online on XLinkDB at http://xlinkdb.gs.washington.edu/xlinkdb/PHP_SAVED_VIEWS/hwippel/HeLa_BDP_NHP_Bruce.php. An interaction network was generated with crosslinks (i) of the whole dataset and (ii) including only crosslinks of RBPs (Supplementary material 3). Supplementary material 2 shows the overlap between crosslink identifications and proteins from the two replicates. The low overlap of replicates is likely due to stochastic sampling with mass spectrometry due to low duty cycle for cross-linked peptide analysis that requires multiple stages of high resolution acquisition. . The structure modeling and interactome analysis of hnRNP proteins hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, hnRNPC, and RALY are discussed in the following sections.
Investigating the structure and interactome of hnRNPs

Crosslinks for hnRNP proteins were detected using the XL-MS strategy (Figure 2). By combing the intralink information with available protein structures, using comprising RBDs, we generated modeled structures for the hnRNPs investigated here – hnRNPC. hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, RALY – that are involved in the regulation of pre-mRNA splicing. The interlinks between hnRNPs and ribosomal proteins RpL18, RpS3, RpL13, and annexin A2, albeit being part of the crosslinking interactome, are not discussed in this study.
hnRNPC

hnRNPC (UniProt HNRPC_HUMAN), besides having a role in the splicing of pre-mRNAs in the nucleus, is part of the 40S hnRNP complex and binds to regulatory regions of pre-mRNAs – poly-uridine regions in the 3’-untranslated regions (UTR) or 5’-UTR – to modulate the target transcripts stability, localization, and translation rates. This protein is a stable tetramer in solution, with a (C1)3C2 organization; the C2 is the canonical version of the protein, while C1 is an alternatively spliced variant missing amino acids 108 to 120. hnRNPC has regulatory regions in its sequence (Figure 3b), including one RRM domain, a nuclear localization signal (NLS), and aspartic acid (Asp, D)/glutamic acid (Glu, E)-rich motif, involved in mRNA processing and regulation.

The majority of the intralinks found in the RRM domain of hnRNPC were identified in the RNP1 consensus motif, residues 50 to 57 with sequence KGFAFVQY, with crosslinked lysine K50 (Supplementary material 1; Figure 3). The RNP2 consensus motif comprises residues 18–23, with sequence VFIGNL, with one intralink identified nearby this region and the RNP1 (K29_K50). These motifs are related to the specificity of protein-mRNA binding and are highly conserved in RRM domains. We show a representative set of MS1/MS2 spectra of hnRNPC PIR-crosslinked peptides K157_K50 (AVVPSK157R_IVGCSVHK50GFAFVQYVNER) (Figure 4). The identification of crosslinks in this region indicates solvent accessibility of the motif, being an exposed surface and available for RNA binding. Interestingly, the β-sheets of the two RRM domains of hnRNPA1 are more likely to be exposed to solvent and form a RNA binding accessible surface, according to a crystal structure of the domains. Furthermore, these intralinks improve understanding of the conformation and structure of hnRNPC. Considering that hnRNPC has a highly disordered C-terminus region and the PDB structures available using the NMR method only include a coiled-coil region and the RRM domain, the modelling of the protein structure was done using a Phyre2 intensive mode. The top ranked result, i.e., best alignment result, was the crystal structure of the splicing factor SFPQ (PDB 4WIJA), with 13% of sequence identity with hnRNPC (Supplementary material 5). We note that intrinsically disordered proteins, like hnRNPC, usually only have structure upon protein interactions, thus justifying the modeling of the disordered region coupled with the domains structure.

Many intralinks shown in Figure 3a have distances over 35 Å. This is indicative of change in conformation or structural organization, since 95% of BDP crosslinks mapped against known structures link lysine residues 35 Å apart or less, with distance measured between the alpha carbons of two linked residues. The Phyre2 modeling results of hnRNPC show that the crystal structure of SFPQ (PDB 4WIJ) is the most similar to hnRNPC, with 99% of homology confidence. Hence, the structure of the dimer of SFPQ was used to represent a dimer structure of hnRNPC (Figure 3c, Table 1). Then, the crosslink distances were evaluated in this antiparallel organization of hnRNPC as a dimer. The protein sequence alignment provided by Phyre2 was used to identify residues in SFPQ that aligned with crosslinked sites in hnRNPC. Indeed, the intralinks with distances over 35 Å in the monomer structure were observed to be less than 35 Å when mapped against the dimer structure (Figure 3c). This modeling is corroborated by a previous publication showing the antiparallel arrangement of the coiled-coil region of hnRNPC (residues 194–220) in the oligomerization domain tetramer, the same conformation of SFPQ shown in Figure 3c.

The splicing factor hnRNPA1 (UniProt ROA1_HUMAN) is the most abundant protein of the hnRNP family in the nucleus. It interacts with pre-mRNAs to form hnRNPs and controls the processing, stability, subcellular localization, and transport of mature transcripts to the cytoplasm. This protein is part of the spliceosomal C complex and is involved in spliceosome assembly. hnRNPA1 also has a role in inhibiting the alternative splicing of its target pre-mRNAs, besides repressing the CAP-independent translation of mature mRNAs. Although hnRNPA1 abundantly localizes in the nucleus, it shuttles between the nucleus and the cytoplasm via the M9 nuclear transport signal transporting mature mRNAs. In addition to the two RRMs in the N-terminus region, hnRNPA1 has other regulatory and RNA-binding sites in its sequence (Figure 5b). These include (i) a tri-arginine-glycine-glycine (RGG) motif, involved in transcription, pre-mRNA splicing, DNA damage signaling, mRNA translation, regulation of apoptosis, and RNA-protein and protein-protein interactions; (ii) the M9 nuclear transport signal (NTS), responsible for the shuttling of hnRNPA1 between nucleus and cytoplasm, transporting mature mRNAs; and (iii) a glycine (Gly)-rich region in the C-terminus region, involved in binding to nucleotides (DNA/RNA) (Figure 5b). hnRNPA1 stabilizes as tetramer in solution with a (A1)3B2 organization, B2 being the canonical isoform and A1 an alternative isoform with residues 252 to 303 missing.

Available hnRNPA1 structures contain only the RRM domains and the structure shown here resulted from a docking using PatchDock between (i) the PDB 1HA1 for the RRM1/2 domains and (ii) the disordered region (185–372) of a hnRNPA1 modelled structure using the Phyre2 intensive mode (Figure 5a). The crosslinking between the RRMs and the M9 NTS (residue K350), located in the non-ordered region of the protein, were used to guide docking of the two separate regions of the protein (Supplementary material 1 and online interaction table). The RRMs followed by a Gly-rich region in the structure of hnRNPA1 enable it to bind other proteins and nucleic acids, being key for the mechanisms of packaging nascent RNAs and the nuclear and cytoplasmic mRNA processing and metabolism. The crosslinks between the RRMs and the M9 NTS (located in the Gly-rich region in the C-terminus end) indicate these regions are proximal to one another at some point in side cells. Interestingly, all the interlinks identified for hnRNPA1, including the hnRNPC (Figure 8a), occurred in the M9 NTS, suggesting a role of this sequence in protein-protein interaction and complex assembly for nuclear shuttling.

In contrast to hnRNPC, the intralinks inside the RRMs have distances under 35 Å, indicating agreement between the crystal structure of the domains and the crosslinking information (Figure 5a). These results illustrate how cross-linking data can complement conventional structural techniques to increase insight on disordered regions. Moreover, future efforts to incorporate quantitative cross-linking can reveal how links and interactions between subunits and domains are perturbed under various conditions to further elucidate conformational features and flexibility in disordered proteins.

hnRNPA2/B1 is part of the 40S hnRNP particle and interacts with nascent target transcripts with high specificity and mediates their packing into hnRNPs in the nucleus. Similarly to hnRNPA1, this protein plays a role in several cellular processes, including transcription, pre-mRNA processing, RNA nuclear export, subcellular location, translation, and stability of mature mRNAs. hnRNPA2/B1 regulates the efficiency of mRNA splicing, possibly by binding to N6-methyladenosine (m6A)-containing pre-mRNAs, in addition to mediating the processing of pre-microRNAs. Moreover, hnRNPA1 and hnRNPA2/B1 have a high level of amino acid sequence identity, especially in their domains and motifs – 80% for the RRMs and 58% for the Gly-rich region, that could indicate a similarity in protein function.

The conserved regulatory sequences of hnRNPA2 comprise a nuclear localization signal (NLS) in the N-terminus region, two RRMs, a Gly-rich region in the C-terminus (Figure 6b). hnRNPA2/B1 has a (A2)3B1 tetramer organization in solution; B1 is the canonical isoform and isoform A2 lacks the residues 3 to 14, that includes the NLS. The hnRNPA2 structure shown here, PDB 5EN1, comprises only the two RRM domains and was selected because, in contrast to hnRNPA1, no crosslinks were identified outside the RRMs (Figure 6a). All crosslinks show distances under 35 Å, consistent with the conformation in the crystal structure of the RRMs (PDB 5EN1).
hnRNP RALY

The RBP associated with lethal yellow mutation (RALY) binds poly-uridine (U) rich elements of RNAs and regulates the expression and the stability of its target transcripts. It is also part of the spliceosomal C complex, regulating the splicing of nascent transcripts, and acts in the processing of a specific subset of miRNAs (miR-483, miR-676, and miR-877). RALY has also been reported as being involved in the tumorigenesis of lung cancer and inducing metastasis in breast cancer by mediating the alternative splicing of an isoform of the arginine methyltransferase 1.

RALY has a RRM domain in the N-terminus region and a Poly-Gly sequence, implicated in RNA-binding activity (Figure 7b). The RALY protein structure shown here was generated by Phyre2 modeling on intensive mode, with 72% of the sequence disordered (Figure 7a). We note that RBPs are usually enriched in disordered regions and that these sequences are involved in transcription regulation and RNA processing and metabolism. The only crosslink identified for RALY in the present work includes residue 55, part of the RRM domain, and this site was identified in an interlink between RALY and hnRNPC (Figure 8c).
hnRNP interactome

In this study, interlinks between hnRNPC and hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, and RALY were detected (Supplementary material 1; Figure 8). The interlink between hnRNPC and hnRNPA1 was identified linking lysine residues K42 and K350, respectively (Figure 8a). These two residues are present in regulatory regions of the proteins: the RRM domain of hnRNPC and the shuttling signal M9 NTS of hnRNPA1. Along with the intralinks of hnRNPA1, which indicates a proximity of the M9 NTS with the two RRMs (Figure 5), the RRM of hnRNPC and the M9 signal of hnRNPA1 are close and possibly coordinately acting in the processing (via the RRM) and export (via the M9 NTS) of mRNAs from the nucleus to the cytoplasm. The proximity of hnRNPC to hnRNPA2/B1 is indicated by the crosslinking of the residues K42 and K94, respectively (Figure 8b). As was observed with hnRNPA1, the residue K42 within the RRM of hnRNPC is interlinked with hnRNPA2/B1, but in this case the crosslink happens with its RRM1. hnRNPA2/B1 has a NTS in its sequence (Figure 6b), but no interlinks between its disordered region (residues 202–353) were identified in our results. However, the proximity of RRMs of these two proteins may suggest a concomitant and shared regulation of target transcripts, since the RNA-binding domains seem to be close to each other (modeled distance under 24 Å, Figure 8b).

The crosslinking between residues K55 of RALY and K157 of hnRNPC indicates the proximity between the RBPs (Figure 8c). The presence of RALY and hnRNPC in the same complex has already been reported by the literature in a study using in vivo-biotinylation-pulldown-quant (iBioPQ) approach, but the results here are the first illustrating their direct physical interaction and enable binding surfaces to be models based on crosslink-directed docking. The lysine K55 of RALY is part of the RRM domain and was linked to the nuclear localization signal (NLS) of hnRNPC, indicating the proximity of these two motifs that may be important for transport of mature mRNAs and also the shuttling of the protein to the cytoplasm.

Interestingly, crosslinking results presented in this study indicate that hnRNPC appears to hold a central role when interacting with hnRNPA1, hnRNPA2/B1, and RALY, acting as a core or hub of the complex, since all the interlinks found had hnRNPC as the common factor.

We note that hnRNPs act in other regulatory processes as well, such as the regulation of translation and mRNA stabilization. The results shown here, together with those discussed above, bring a new level of discussion about how hnRNPs proteins interact in their complexes to regulate RNAs. While significant discussion exists in the current literature about RNP components that have been identified with a variety of technologies, most of them include different types of fractionation or isolation, and none reveal physical contact surfaces to shed light on RBP interacting regions to better understand molecular function. Moreover, the crosslinks found in RNA-binding domains and other regulatory regions of the RBPs discussed here indicate solvent accessibility and, consequently, RNA-binding availability.
XL-MS for the study of EnigmRBPs

EnigmRBPs comprise a class of proteins with evidence of RNA-binding activity, but which lack any conserved RNA-binding domain or known relation to RNA biology. Much is yet to be discovered on the interactome and structural organization of these proteins when regulating RNA metabolism. The chemical crosslinking of enigmRBPs could provide new insights into protein-protein interactions of enigmRBPs. Using the protein identifiers from Beckmann et al., we filtered the crosslinking interaction table on XLinkDB for enigmRBPs. A total of 312 crosslinks were detected for enigmRBPs, with 28% interlinks, corresponding to 286 site pairs and 111 protein pairs (Supplementary material 6, interaction table at http://xlinkdb.gs.washington.edu/xlinkdb/PHP_SAVED_VIEWS/hwippel/EnigmRBPs_Bruce.php). The Gene Ontology analysis, embedded on XLinkDB, showed an enrichment for molecular functions related to RNA binding (72 proteins), protein binding (21 proteins), ATP binding (20 proteins), cadherin binding (20 proteins), and actin binding (16 proteins). Biological processes are related to neutrophil degranulation, negative regulation of apoptotic process, protein folding, viral process, and nucleosome assembly. Interestingly, histones are part of nucleosomes and considered enigmRBPs, with involvement in alternative splicing regulation. Here, we detected 109 crosslinks for histones, including inter and intralinks (Supplementary material 6).

Interlinks between proteins that comprise the Ku antigen complex, XRCC5 and XRCC6, were detected with the XL-MS strategy applied in this study. This complex is involved in the repair of DNA double-strand breaks, and its dysregulation is linked to systemic lupus erythematosus. The crosslinks happen between regulatory regions of the proteins: the Ku and the DNA-binding SAP domains of XRCC6 and the leucine-zipper and Ku domains of XRCC5 (Figure 9). The three interlink distances agree with an available crystal structure of the XRCC5/XRCC6 heterodimer (PDB 1JEQ), all under 35 Å (Figure 9a, interaction table on XLinkDB). The crosslinking between regulatory regions of enigmRBPs are an evidence of the usefulness of XL-MS as a large-scale tool for the analysis of these proteins, providing insights into their interactome and structure information.

For the LC-MS/MS analysis, 3 μL of each sample (approximately 1 μg) from each pooled fraction was injected into the nano-LC system (Thermo), coupled to a Q-Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo). Each fraction was analyzed 2 times for technical replicates of the experiment. Each peptide fraction was then loaded onto a trap column [3 cm × 100-μm i.d., stationary phase ReproSil-Pur C8 (5-μm diameter and 120-Å-pore-size particles)] with a flow rate of 2 μL/min of mobile phase: 98% (vol/vol) LC–MS solvent A [0.1% (vol/vol) FA in water] and 2% (vol/vol) LC–MS solvent B [0.1% (vol/vol) FA in acetonitrile], and chromatographically separated using an analytical column [60 cm × 75-μm i.d., stationary phase ReproSil-Pur C8 (5-μm diameter and 120-Å-pore-size particles)], applying a 240-min linear gradient: from 95% LC–MS solvent A, 5% LC–MS solvent B to 60% LC–MS solvent A, 40% LC–MS solvent B, at a flow rate of 300 nL/min. For Mango analysis of the PIR crosslinker, the mass spectrometer was set to high resolution method to data-dependent acquisition (DDA) of the 5 most intense ions with charge state of +4 to +8, with a dynamic exclusion of 30 s and isolation window of 3 Da. Each MS1 scan (70,000 resolving power at 200 m/z, automated gain control (AGC) of 1 × 106, scan range 400 to 2,000 m/z, dynamic exclusion of 30 s) was followed by 5 MS2 scans (70,000 resolving power at 200 m/z, AGC of 5 × 104, normalized collision energy of 30).
Data Analysis

LC-MS/MS data files in.RAW format were converted to .mzXML format using the ReADW tool, followed by Mango analysis (freely available at https://github.com/jpm369/mango), to generate .ms2 files containing individual precursor masses of released peptides for each spectrum and .peaks file containing all relationships within a 20 ppm tolerance. Comet was used to search the.mzXML files against the human database downloaded from Uniprot on January 1st 2019, containing both forward and reverse protein sequences. The search results were validated using XLinkProphet, available at https://github.com/brucelab/xlinkprophet, on the pep.xml files resulted from the Comet search to apply a 1% FDR value. The results were uploaded to XLinkDB, available on XLinkDB at http://xlinkdb.gs.washington.edu/xlinkdb/PHP_SAVED_VIEWS/hwippel/HeLa_BDP_NHP_Bruce. We used Gene Ontology analysis, embedded on XLinkDB, to filter the interaction table for RBPs.
Molecular docking

Phyre2 and PatchDock were used for the modeling and docking of the RBPs structures, respectively. The hnRNPC structure was modelled using Phyre2 on intensive mode, with 99% of residues modelled at >90% confidence, with 75% of the sequence disordered. The alignment between the hnRNPC protein sequence and the PDB 4WIJ of the SFPQ protein had 13% of sequence identity, with 99% of homology confidence. For hnRNPA1, the structure resulted from a docking using PatchDock between (i) the PDB 1HA1 for the RRM1/2 domains and (ii) the disordered region (185–372) of a hnRNPA1 modelled structure using the Phyre2 intensive mode. The hnRNPA2 structure (PDB 5EN1) comprises only the two RRM domains. The RALY protein structure was generated by Phyre2 modeling on intensive mode, with 41% of residues modelled at >90% confidence, with 72% of the sequence disordered; the alignment between the RALY protein sequence and the PDB 1WF1 had 99.9% confidence and 94% identity.
DATA AVAILABILITY

The datasets generated during this study are available on XLinkDB at http://xlinkdb.gs.washington.edu/xlinkdb/PHP_SAVED_VIEWS/hwippel/HeLa_BDP_NHP_Bruce.php. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD023577.
CONCLUSION

Despite RBP research community efforts, much is yet to be discovered of the world of RBPs and how they cooperate to regulate their target transcripts. hnRNPs comprise a family of nuclear RBPs that are involved in the regulation of many nuclear processes, including alternative splicing. The use of chemical crosslinking shed light not only on hnRNP structures and interactions, but also help reveal what specific regions are interacting to regulate different cellular processes. The next step on the field of RBPs exploration would be to use chemical crosslinking of proteins incorporated with the widely used UV crosslinking (for RNA-protein interactions). Coupled with the poly-A enrichment, it would possible to identify crosslinks of proteins that are linked to RNA. Overall, the crosslinking pipeline used here to study interactions and structure of RBPs is a foundation for significantly improved understanding of RBP complexes and their mechanisms of RNA regulation.
